messages.subject: micro_era5 shading ranges
parts:
Hello,

Background:
I am modeling the microclimate of a grasshopper in meadow sites along an elevational gradient in Colorado. Ultimately, I am and trying to find a range of different body temperatures (Tbs) the hopper could thermoregulate to. (As far as thermoregulation, I am doing my own rather coarse thing by letting them move towards their preferred body temperature with no energetic cost. I am not using any of the biophysical modeling capabilities of NicheMapR -- just microclimate.)

My workflow is era5 data -> micro_era5 microclimate data at different combinations of height and shading -> Tb (using the TrenchR package)

Question:
My issue right now is that I think I am getting too wide of a range of microclimates, particularly air temperatures (varying as a result of shading) and I don't know how to address it.

I'll talk a little bit more about my approach now. I represent 5 different possible microclimates based on a combination of height above the ground and degree of shading: four combinations of what I consider the "extremes" -- 1) 0.005m above the ground (so, on the soil) and no shading, 2) 0.005m above the ground and 90% shading, 3) 0.15m above the ground and no shading, 5) 0.15m above the ground and 90% shading -- and a more intermediate position 5) 0.03m above the ground and 30% shading (this one is excluded from the figure in my reprex just to keep things simple, but the data is there). 

[Side note: For thermoregulation, I will calculate the Tb at each of these 5 microclimates and let the maximum and minimum Tb at each hour define the range of possible Tbs. Then the hopper can move as close as the range allows to their preferred body temperature of ~35C (so if the range includes 35C, their Tb is 35C.)]

I am getting a wider range of air temperatures than I would have expected (~10C in the sunniest part of the day) and I imagine the range of available Tbs will be quite broad in the middle of the day. Did I implement something wrong? Or was 90% shading too aggressive of an option (I was imagining a hopper still in a meadow -- not a forest -- but seeking shade under some vegetation)? (I can also see how 0.005m above the ground is going to be rather driven by soil temperature, but I am trying to represent grasshoppers that are on the ground.)

Reprex:
I've attached an image and a zipfile with a simplified reprex. Here is some more info regarding that:
1. Rplot.png: a little info in addition to what's in the legend... the brown lines represent soil surface temperatures (at different levels of shading), while the other lines represent air temperatures (at different heights above the ground and at different levels of shading)
2. The zipfile contains 3 .R files that are run in the following order (also contains their outputs, already generated for you... you may want to start by running the 3rd file to check reproduce the figure and look at the dataframe)
a) ERA5Downloader.R uses mcera5 to get the ERA data as .nc files
b) get_microclim.R uses micro_era5() to get the 5 microclimates I described above
c) viz_microclim() creates the attached plot 

Thank you so much!

messages.author: 6cec8ea3702ece93
messages.subject: Re: micro_era5 shading ranges
parts:
OK that worked - so, now I'll try and reply:

First thanks for the excellent detail in your question, and sounds like an interesting study. 

When you simulate shade with the microclimate model it is as if you have an infinite plane of shading at that level altering the ground temperature and air temperature profiles. This would be representative of what conditions would be like in e.g. a very large bush or under a canopy. However, in your case of a meadow, because of the small area of shade and the fact that air is mixing, the air temperature would be pretty much the same in and out of the shade. So what I would do is simulate your grasshoppers under the same convective regime (air temp and wind speed) but just cut the solar down by the shade fraction. Depending on how much shade, you could change the long-wave radiation environment from open sky and sunlit ground to be equal to air temperature to account for the fact that the veg is probably roughly air temperature radiating down on the grasshopper (depends how much of the sky the grasshopper 'sees') and the surface of the ground may be cooler than the open ground due to the shade.

You might want to try the micro_usa function in addition to the micro_era5 function, which is based on the USA gridMET dataset and is extracted directly from the web via opendap, so no need to pre-download all the data like with ERA5 (it's daily rather than hourly but higher resolution). Also to save microclimate runs, you can just simulate at one height and then use the get_profile function (see here) to get any other heights you like.

All the best,
Mike
